# Summary of Philip Rubin
Philip Rubin is a prominent psychologist and linguist whose multidisciplinary research integrates computational, engineering, linguistic, physiological, and psychological approaches to understand embodied cognition, particularly focusing on the biological basis of speech and language. He is widely recognized for pioneering work in articulatory synthesis—a computational modeling of speech production—sinewave synthesis, signal processing, perceptual organization, and theoretical modeling of complex temporal events. Rubin designed key software systems at Haskins Laboratories, including ASY (articulatory synthesis program), SWS (sinewave synthesis program), and HADES (signal processing system). He contributed to advancing speech science through collaborations that integrated articulatory phonology, task dynamics, and gesture-based models of speech production. Rubin co-founded the Auditory-Visual Speech Association, now part of the International Speech Communication Association, and helped develop innovative approaches to audiovisual speech and multimodality.
Beyond research, Rubin has held significant leadership roles in science policy and administration, including serving as Director of the Division of Behavioral and Cognitive Sciences at the National Science Foundation and later as Assistant Director for Social, Behavioral, and Economic Sciences at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy. He has been active in science advocacy, ethical oversight of human subjects research, and interdisciplinary initiatives encompassing neuroscience, aging, behavioral science, and forensic science. Rubin is president and chair of the Federation of Associations in Behavioral and Brain Sciences and serves on various boards, including Haskins Laboratories and the University of Connecticut Board of Trustees. His extensive contributions have been recognized through numerous fellowships and awards from leading scientific and professional organizations.
